1- Research Questions¶

Requirements (120 words): In the world of bookworms, being able to tell the different genres of a Light Novel (LN) or a Web Novel (WN) based on its description is very common. Unfortunately, this apparent simplicity represent a quite difficult task for computers. Using the not so known Web/Light Novel Dataset, our goal is to predict, from the description of a book, the associated genre(s). We emits the hypothesis (already used for movies classification) that a description unveils a particular semantic depending on the genres they are associated with. As instance, a LN with the Horror tag is more likely to have a gore description than a Romance/School Life LN. Additionally, we also emit the hypothesis of high correlation between genres (Adventure implies Fantasy or Drama/Romance).

Required Reflection:

[Q1] Why is your research question non trivial? Multiple difficulties arise with this research question, but the two main difficulties are the high number of genres (35 in our dataset), but also their correlation together, which would render discrimination attempt difficult (Note: maybe it correlation could be turn into strength).

[Q2] What linguistic phenomenon does it involve? The linguistics phenomenon involved we want to capture here is the underlying semantics of the different genres. We expect more joyful "words" and sentences structures for genres like Romance/Comedy, more tendentious for Adult/Ecchi/Harem/Gender Bender, more youthful for Shoujo/Shounen/Adventure and so on.

[Q3] What would falsify your hypothesis? A possible justification for our hypothesis being falsified could be that the translation of the description from the original language (Chinese, Korean, Japanese, Vietnamese, ...) to english removed some details and damaged the underlying semantics.

2.1 - Dataset Selection¶

The dataset chosen for this project is the Web/Light Novel Dataset (original-wn-dataset.csv).

  • Source: Kaggle, Web/Light Novel Dataset, Prem Shinde, 2024
  • Domain: Literature, Web/Light Novels, Asian Literature
  • Label Distribution: Multilabel, Heterogeneous (some labels have 106, others 7523), "exponential" unbalanced distributions of labels.
  • Potential biases: Correlation between books origins and labels, correlation between labels, traduction failures of Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, ... to English.
  • Ethical Consideration: Methodology for extraction is unknown. Apart from this, this dataset does not exhibit particular ethicals considerations.
  • Size: 11770 labeled documents, 74.87MB.
  • Main Content: Title, Description [Classifiers], Source (URL), Genres [Predicted variable], Tags (Sub genres), related series, authors, artists, original language...

Despite relatively poor documentation, this dataset was chosen as it is more complete (more instances) in comparison with other available alternative, possess a bigger variety of genres and tags, but also is easier to navigate. Alternative could have been:

  • RanobeDB: SQL Database containing series and books for manga, LN and WN. (difficult to navigate),
  • MyAnimeList Dataset: Very complete and good documentation, but has less variety and may not contains LN and WN independent productions.
  • Anime Title Dataset: Complete, but has very low number of instances (<1000) and Anime Only.

More informations on the shape of the dataset in the part (2.1 - In Depth)

Preprocess Dataset Format¶

Using the .head() command, we observe that the genres and tags columns are encoded into space separated list, which are not recognised in Python, so we will have to change the format to proper lists.

In [4]:
def colToList (x:str) -> list[str]:
    # Detect the separator
    x = re.sub(r"'[\n ].?'", ",",x)
    
    # Remove the indicator of the raw space separated list and split on coma
    xSplit = x.removeprefix("['").removesuffix("']").split(",")
    
    # Return the list where the text is capitalize (it is just prettier)
    return list(map(str.capitalize, xSplit))

# Apply the split
df_filtered.loc[:,"genres"] = df_filtered.loc[:,"genres"].apply(lambda x: colToList(x))
df_filtered.loc[:,"tags"] = df_filtered.loc[:,"tags"].apply(lambda x: colToList(x))

2.1bis (and 3.1.) - in depth - Some stats on the dataset¶

Now that everything is correctly imported, we will observe some statistics on our dataset to understand it. First, we will try to understand what kind of language is used in our data.

Description language¶

To achieve this goal, we will first take a look at the most frequent words in our dataset. We will build a function to compare with and without stopwords.

In [5]:
def plotDescriptionLanguage(df:pd.DataFrame, col="description", stopFiltered=True):
    descriptionList = list(map(str,df.loc[:,col].to_list()))
    descriptionString = " ".join(descriptionList)
    # Match all words and digits
    wordDescriptionList = re.findall(r"[\w\d-]+",descriptionString)

    # Remove the stopwords if asked
    wordDescriptionList = [i.capitalize() for i in wordDescriptionList if (i.lower() not in stop_words) or not stopFiltered]

    # Apply the counter
    wordDescriptionListCounter = Counter(wordDescriptionList)

    # Sort the counter
    wordDescriptionListCounterSorted = [[],[]]
    for word in sorted(wordDescriptionListCounter, key=lambda x:wordDescriptionListCounter[x], reverse=True):
        wordDescriptionListCounterSorted[0].append(word)
        wordDescriptionListCounterSorted[1].append(wordDescriptionListCounter[word])

    # Make a plot
    plt.close("all")
    sns.set_style("dark")
    sns.barplot(
        x=wordDescriptionListCounterSorted[1][:40],
        y=wordDescriptionListCounterSorted[0][:40],
        palette="BrBG"    
    )
    plt.title(f"Wordcount {'(stopwords filtered)' if stopFiltered else ''}")
    plt.xlabel("Wordcount")
    plt.ylabel("Words")

    plt.show()
    
    return wordDescriptionListCounterSorted

Now that we have the function, we can start without stopwords filtering:

Here, using the table, we observe that the nature of least used words could be categorised (broadly) in four categories: composed words (Strength-worshiping, Adult-based, Good-nature), names (Tsuruki, Zhaoying, Ikaros), specialised words (Euthanasia, Canines, Serializing) or non-English components (Otouto, Giraffe, 100g, 1920, 房事).

Additionally, we observe that 22603 unique words (55.10%) appears less than 2 times and that even 16732 words (40.78%) appears only once. This observation will render necessary to filter rare words.

In the end, the proportion of words that could be considered "frequent" (20 words or more) is of approximately 12.3%. Concerning "very frequent words" (100+ occurrences), only 3.64% of them can be considered that way. We can therefore clearly see the concentration in occurrences and the heterogeneity of the dictionary used.

Here we observe that some genres are really underrepresented. It is the case for Sport, Gender Bender, Wuxia and Mecha. In consequence, we will simply remove the labels in the dataset to facilitate our prediction.

Additionally, we are in the context where some tags are really close together and could be interchangeable. For example the tags Shounen AI and Yaoi are defined in the same way, but the focus is on the relationship within the boy-loves for the first and on more tendentious activities for the second (I do not read such things, so I could have made a mistake, but it is what results after some research on Internet). With different semantics, we can also have the same interchangeability remarks with the following genres:

  • Smut vs Adult,
  • Xuanhuan vs Xianxia
  • Yuri vs Shoujo AI
  • Yaoi vs Shounen AI

For the genres concerned, we will simply merge them.

In [12]:
# Dictionary of interchangeable genres
transferGenres = {
    "Smut":"Adult",
    "Shoujo ai":"Yuri",
    "Xianxia":"Xuanhuan",
    "Shounen ai":"Yaoi"
}
# Genres to remove
forbiddenGenres = set([
    "Sports",
    "Wuxia",
    "Mecha",
    "Gender bender"
])

# For each document
dfGenresFiltered = []
for genres in df_filtered.loc[:,"genres"]:
    genres_copy:list = genres.copy()
    
    # Changes the genres by removing/transforming the labels
    for genre in genres:
        if genre in forbiddenGenres:
            genres_copy.remove(genre)
        if genre in transferGenres:
            genres_copy.remove(genre)
            genres_copy.append(transferGenres[genre])
    dfGenresFiltered.append(genres_copy)

df_genresFiltered = df_filtered.copy(deep=True)
df_genresFiltered.loc[:, "genres"] = pd.Series(dfGenresFiltered)

# Create the genre id dictionary
genreToGenreID = {genre:label for label, genre in enumerate(set(genresList))}
genreIDtoGenre = {value:key for key, value in genreToGenreID.items()}

# Create the genreCount dictionary
genreMatrix = np.zeros((len(genreIDtoGenre),len(genreIDtoGenre)), dtype=int)

## For all genres
for genres in df_genresFiltered.loc[:,"genres"].tolist():
    # If it is the only genre, then loop to itself
    if len(genres)==1:
        genreMatrix[genreToGenreID[genres[0]], genreToGenreID[genres[0]]] += 1
        continue
    # Otherwise, add a link to all couple of genre which are different
    for genre1 in genres:
        for genre2 in genres:
            if genre1 != genre2:
                genreMatrix[genreToGenreID[genre1], genreToGenreID[genre2]] += 1

# Make the graph for visibility
G = nx.from_numpy_array(genreMatrix)
G = nx.relabel_nodes(G, dict(enumerate(list(genreToGenreID.keys()))))

# Compute the weights of each edges for the graph
weights = np.array(list(nx.get_edge_attributes(G,"weight").values()))
weights = weights/weights.max()

# Compute the degree of each node to infer nodes sizes
deg = dict(G.degree(weight="weight"))
node_sizes = [100 + 400 * deg[n] / max(deg.values()) for n in G.nodes()]

# Plot the graph
plt.close("all")
nx.draw_networkx(
                 G,                         # The graph 
                 pos=nx.shell_layout(G),    # The layout
                 width=3*weights,           # The width of the edges
                 edge_color=weights,        # Edge colour defined by the weights
                 edge_cmap=plt.cm.GnBu,     # Colour map of the edges
                 font_size="x-small",       # The font size
                 font_color="black",        # The font colour
                 font_weight="bold",        # We want bold
                 font_family="Arial",       # We want Arial
                 node_size=node_sizes,      # The size of the nodes
                 edgecolors="black",        # The border colour of the nodes
                 linewidths=1.2,            # Contour colour of the nodes
                 node_color=node_sizes,     # Colour of the node depends on the degree

)

Here we observe some high correlation between genres which are going to either hinder our work or increase our predictive power depending on our classifications. For example, we have the triad Adventure, Fantasy and Action frequently appearing so if we have the two first, we could have a high chance of having the last.

In the end, the extensive study on the genres, allowed us to remove 8 of the original labels, letting us works from 35 genres to 27 genres.

2.2 - Data Split¶

In this subpart we discuss data split strategies considering our multilabel situation. Indeed, in our case, doing a classic 60-20-20 split or a stratified split is not necessarily a good choice since multiple labels can appears, thus making balanced division difficult.

A first idea was to make a training-dev-test set for each possible labels, but this would mix the training/test data from one classifier to another while completely avoiding interdependence is impossible in our context.

This is why we will use scikit multilearn iterative_train_test_split function as suggested on the Data Science Stack Exchange, which provide an optimised version of the classical train test split for multilabel. Note that, in opposition with standard train-test split method, the iterative method, described by Konstantinos Sechidis et al. in the paper On the Stratification of Multi-label Data, is usually deterministic and aims to conserve the balance of the different labels in the produced sets.

Unfortunately, in case of ties, the break is done randomly. From scikit multilearn version 0.2.0, the function implemented in scikit multilearn does not enable us to fix the state. In consequence, we will temporarily fix the state globally using np.random.seed (after checking, it seems to work). For simplicity and time constraint, we will evaluate our model on the tie-breaking seed = 0 for training/dev-test split and seed = 42 for dev/test split. Considering the nature of the split method, which is mostly deterministic, this should not have huge consequences.

In our situation, where we have a lot of classes and a decently sized dataset, we will use a 75-15-10 repartition.

In [18]:
# To use the function: https://github.com/scikit-multilearn/scikit-multilearn/discussions/282

# Transform our labels lists into dummy classifier
mlb = MultiLabelBinarizer()
Y = mlb.fit_transform(df_genresFiltered.loc[:,"genres"].tolist())

# Transform our X into something working
X = df_genresFiltered[["description"]].to_numpy()
X = X[..., np.newaxis]

# Register the id of each labels (column of y)
labelIdtoLabelName = {i:label for i, label in enumerate(mlb.classes_)}
labelNameToLabelId = {v:k for k,v in labelIdtoLabelName.items()}


# Train Dev Test Split
## Train Test Split (0.75 training)
## Ensure reproducibility globally
np.random.seed(0)
X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test = iterative_train_test_split(X, Y, test_size = 0.25)
## Test Dev split (0.6*0.25=0.15 dev and 0.4*0.25 = 0.1 test)
np.random.seed(42)
X_test, y_test, X_dev, y_dev = iterative_train_test_split(X_test, y_test, test_size=0.6)

# Reset the seed
np.random.seed(None)

# Print some informations:
print(
f"""
The shape of the training set is {X_train.shape},
the shape of the test set is {X_test.shape},
the shape of the dev set is {X_dev.shape}
"""
)

The shape of the training set is (8765, 1, 1),
the shape of the test set is (1210, 1, 1),
the shape of the dev set is (1795, 1, 1)

2.3 - Preprocessing Strategies¶

In this section, we will justify our preprocessing choices as bullet-points and justification format:

  • Tokenization Method: Word-level tokenization. We do not plan on using transformers in our multilabel context; indeed, this approach would be too time-consuming without a GPU, this is why we will stick with classical ML techniques such as tf-idf, Bayes, Logistic regressions and pre-trained embeddings like GloVe, which is not trained on subwords. Additionally, in section 2.1bis, we observed many composed word in rare occurrences; in consequence, we will remove the hyphen between the composed word to dilute those into separate tokens. Also, the words are going to be lowercased to uniform the different version of the same word.
  • Lemmatization vs Stemming: In our case, where we hypothesize that the context of a label was present in the semantics of the tokens and that we can handle higher time complexity (texts are not too long), we chose to use Lemmatization. Indeed, it could yield better results than stemming because its system is context-aware in opposition to Stemming.
  • Stopwords strategy: In section 2.1bis, we observed that classical stop-words (A, The, To, And, ...) are very frequent without transporting a particular meaning. In this situation, we will use the nltk english stopwords set to filter them.
  • Rare word strategy: In the section 2.1bis, we unravelled that more than half the words are very rare and/or specialised. In this context, we could use tf-idf to detect less important words to filter them based on a proportion or a threshold.
  • Handling of emoji and punctuation: Since we are not in a sentiment analysis case, emoji (which almost inexistant in our dataset) and punctuation does not unveil a particularly strong semantics. We will therefore remove them. The same will be made for numbers in general.

Now that is being said, we can now preprocess our dataset:

In [19]:
def preprocess(string:str, morphologicalAnalysis:bool = False) -> np.ndarray[str]:
    # Preprocess the string using SpaCy and en_cor_web_sm
    string = nlp(str(string))
    
    # If morphological analysis, stop here
    if morphologicalAnalysis:
        return string
    
    # Get the lemma from the 
    lemmatisedString = " ".join([token.lemma_ for token in string])
    
    # Match all words that are not digits. Match accentuated characters and words with apostrophes (don't, won't ,...)
    strings = re.findall(r"[^\W\d_]+(?:'[^\W\d_]+)*", lemmatisedString)
    
    # Return and remove stop words
    return [word.lower() for word in strings if word.lower() not in stop_words]

# Just so that we know the time spent for preprocessing
begin = time.time()

# Preprocess the test set
preprocessedX_test = [preprocess(X_test[i,0,0]) for i in range(X_test.shape[0])]
print(f"Preprocessing of Test Set done! [{X_test.shape[0]} in {time.time()-begin:.4f}s]")
begin = time.time()

# Preprocess the dev set
preprocessedX_dev = [preprocess(X_dev[i,0,0]) for i in range(X_dev.shape[0])]
print(f"Preprocessing of Dev Set done! [{X_dev.shape[0]} in {time.time()-begin:.4f}s]")
begin = time.time()

# Preprocess the training set
preprocessedX_train = [preprocess(X_train[i,0,0]) for i in range(X_train.shape[0])]
print(f"Preprocessing of Train Set done! [{X_train.shape[0]} in {time.time()-begin:.4f}s]")

Now that we have successfully preprocessed the text, we should now tokenize it. For that, we will first form the vocabulary on the training set.

In [20]:
# Counter of word from training set
trainingWordCounter = Counter(chain.from_iterable(preprocessedX_train))

# Get a vectorizer
vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
    tokenizer = lambda x: x, # Input as tokens
    preprocessor = lambda x: x, # Skip preprocessing (already done)
    token_pattern = None # Disable tokenizer (we already have tokens) 
)

# Get TfIdf
preprocessingTFIDFMatrix = vectorizer.fit_transform(preprocessedX_train)

# Get the vocabulary mapping
trainingVocab = vectorizer.vocabulary_
inversedTrainingVocab = {v:k for k,v in trainingVocab.items()}

# Get the initial size of the training vocabulary
print(f"Size of the vocabulary: {len(trainingVocab)}")

Size of the vocabulary: 26449

From now on, we have the base vocabulary. But it is still too large, even though we passed from 41,025 token in the whole dataset to 26,449 just by removing stopwords, lemmatizing and taking the training set vocabulary only.

To solve this issue, we will impose a threshold on the average tf-idf per tokens. Indeed, tokens of less importance would have tendencies to possess lower tf-idf.

In [21]:
# The minimal threshold on tf-idf for which a token is not considered rare anymore. 
# This threshold is purely arbitrary and could be used as an hyperparameter if the time/Processing time is on our side
# This threshold was chose to observe token that are not atrociously rare while being important in the semantics. By this
# threshold, we have approximately 2.2k vocabulary size, which is also reasonable for our system. 
threshold = 0.0005 #0.0005

# Get the vocab above the threshold in term of average tf-idf
filteredVocabID = np.argwhere(preprocessingTFIDFMatrix.mean(axis=0)>threshold)[:,1]
filterVocab = set([inversedTrainingVocab[i] for i in filteredVocabID])

# Plot the results of the selection
pd.DataFrame(
    list(sorted([(
        vocab, 
        trainingWordCounter[vocab],
        preprocessingTFIDFMatrix[:, trainingVocab[vocab]].mean(axis=0).round(6).tolist()[0][0]
    ) for vocab in filterVocab], key=lambda x: x[2], reverse=True)),
    columns=["Token", "Frequency", "Average tf-idf"]
)

From this observation, this seems reasonable. For our second modeling, we will use the GloVe embedding 2024 Wikipedia + Gigaword 5 (11.9B tokens, 1.2M vocab, uncased, 100d vectors, 560 MB download) available here and published in the paper A New Pair of GloVes by Riley Carlson et al.

The particularity of GloVe is that the embedding is capable of understanding the underlying linear structures between words. For example we would have King-Man+Woman approximately equal to Queen. This structure will be useful to provide a document embedding, which we will exploit for classification.

Note (How to download GloVe): when downloaded, unzip it, and place the obtained file in the folder GloVe after renaming it into GloVe2024.txt

In [26]:
# Load GloVe
# Solution adapted from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/37793118/load-pretrained-glove-vectors-in-python
class GloVeClass():
    def __init__(self, path: str):
        self.GloVe = pd.read_table(path, sep=" ", index_col=0, header=None, quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONE)
        self.GloVeMatrix = self.GloVe.to_numpy()
        self.dim = self.GloVe.shape[1]

        # Precompute normalized matrix to make closest word faster
        norms = np.linalg.norm(self.GloVeMatrix, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        self.GloVeMatrixNorm = self.GloVeMatrix / norms

    def closestWord(self, vec: np.ndarray) -> str:
        # Normalise the input vector
        vec_norm = vec / np.linalg.norm(vec)
        
        # Compute cosine similarity as only dot product since it is already normalised (||A||*||B||) 
        cos = np.dot(self.GloVeMatrixNorm, vec_norm)
        
        # Get the index with the highest cosine similarity
        i = np.argmax(cos)
        
        # Get the word
        return self.GloVe.iloc[i].name

    def getVector(self, tokens:list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
        # If the list is empty, return nan for the document embedding
        if len(tokens) == 0:
            return np.full((1, self.dim), np.nan)
        
        # By defaults, embedding is unknown
        result = np.full((len(tokens), self.dim), np.nan)

        # Find which tokens exist
        mask = [t in self.GloVe.index for t in tokens]

        # If tokens exists
        if any(mask):
            # Get the terms
            found_tokens = [t for t, m in zip(tokens, mask) if m]
            
            # Place the vector at the right position
            result[mask] = self.GloVe.loc[found_tokens].to_numpy()

        return result
        
    def getCosineSimilarity(self, vec1:np.ndarray, vec2:np.ndarray) -> float:
        return np.dot(vec1, vec2)/(np.linalg.norm(vec1)*np.linalg.norm(vec2))
        
# Check whether GloVe was well imported
GloVe = GloVeClass(path="GloVe/GloVe2024.txt")

Now back to something serious. Since the underlying structure can be considered captured, we would like to embed all our document using this embedding instead of tf-idf. We will keep the filtering of words though.

Since the presence of unknown embeddings is quite low, we will just ignore them when designing the classifications models.

Concerning the vocabulary size, even though we have initially the same vocabulary size as with tf-idf; in the end, we do not reason on vocabulary anymore, but on vector of fixed length (100). This can be useful as it compress in a way our data.

For the pros and cons of this approach, document embeddings allow us to work on smaller vectors, but also to concentrate the information. The potential drawbacks is clear, the longer the document, the more dilutes the information; fortunately, considering the nature of description (to the point, focused, short text), we should not experience this problem.

We will now answer the thinking questions of this part:

  1. Which preprocessing decision most affects performance? Why?: In our case, the preprocessing decision most affecting the performances are clearly the rare word filtering. Indeed, it is never trivial to fix a clear threshold from which a word should not be took into account. If the threshold is too high, we might not be able to segregate between our data (because of lack of vocabulary), on the opposite spectrum, choosing a low threshold would leads to vocabulary explosion and drastically reduces performances in terms of time and even loss our model focus.
  2. When does aggressive cleaning hurt performance?: If we reduce too much the vocabulary size, it become difficult to classify documents (especially our high proportion of rare words). In our case, having an <oov> proportion higher than it already is could really leads to performances degradation.
  3. Does removing stopwords always help? Provide evidence.: In our case, it helps because description can be seen as full of specialised words. Unfortunately, this is not always the case. For example, saying "This is not important." or "This is important." are clearly opposite, but using nltk stopwords, we would have both as "important". Here we clearly lost the negation semantics.

3 - Exploratory & Linguistic Analysis¶

For the analysis required in this part, you will find in section 2.1bis some interpreted analysis regarding Frequency distributions by class, Dependency structure statistics and Word distribution analysis.

In this part, we will just make a quick reminder of our findings, but please see section 2.1bis for more detailed analysis, this is just a summary.

  • Frequency distributions by class: First, as a reminder, we want to classify our description in the right collection of labels (genres in the datasets) from 35 different genres. From a barplot of genres frequencies, we observed high heterogeneous data with highly present tags (more than half the dataset) such as Romance or Fanatasy. On the opposing spectrum, after a Poisson distributed decrease in occurrences, we get very rare tags like Wuxia, Shojo Ai or Sports with much less than 1% of occurrences. After unravelling this fact, we merged and drop some labels (to reduce time strains for our models, but also to increase the possibility of segregating between classes). Theses drops concerns only low occurrences genres, while merges happen with closely related genres. As a metaphor, if you have a Sofa in your house, it is the same as saying that you have a couch in your house, but you will not say you have both; as such, some genres like Shojo Ai and Yuri basically refers to the same problematic.

  • Dependency structure statistics: Being in a multilabel context, it is important to know how different labels relates to each others. Indeed, it could be useful afterward to know the existences of such relationships for the design of a postprocessing step where we take the correlation into account to enrich our results. In the previously mention section, after dropping/merging genres, we studied the correlation between classes and more precisely how many times does a label appears with another label? In our analysis, we found typical structures of the domain like Fantasy, Action and Adventure bing closely tied together or Fantasy, Comedy and Romance. This is quite interesting, because it could also say that the semantics of the description of these labels are linked. Additionally, we also observe the opposite: genres that does not connect to each other, this is typically the case of Sci-fi, Tragedy or Horror for example, which are almost not linked together in any way.

  • Word Distribution Analysis: In the whole dataset, we observed 1,499,431 words for 41,025 unique and 733,681 stopwords (almost half). This observation, made the usage of stopword imperative in our context to retrieve the real semantics. Additionally, we observed that among the 41,025 unique words, the number of occurrence is also heterogeneous from highly occurring words like World which are related to some genres to least occurring because of differing natures (composed words, specialised or non-english). For the word distribution, we observed that only 12.3% of words are actually frequent (appearing more than 20 time in the whole dataset), but that more than half unique words are occurring only once or twice. In the end, it is important to know this information to form a threshold on the vocabulary size.

Mandatory Linguistic Component¶

For the mandatory component analysis, we will observe if imperative is more used for some classes. As this was done in this post on Stack Overflow, we will identify our imperative form as a verb being at the root of the sentence (as an approximation).

In this plot, we clearly see that no label emerges when comparing an estimate proportion of imperative. This is a bit deceiving, while we could have hypothesise that Action or Martial Arts contains more imperative (for training and so on); but in the end, we did not find any correlation.

In consequence, we can say that in descriptions, imperative does not yield a particular semantics in comparison to other words. This does not break any of our initial hypothesis.

4 - Predictive Modelling¶

4.1 - Baselines¶

Most frequent label baseline (Multinomial Naïve Bayes)¶

In order to make the classifications in the cases of multilabeled data, we will use scikit multilearn as a wrapper for scikit model execution. In a nutshell, instead of training one classifier per columns ourself, we will let skmultilearn do it in order to optimize the processus.

In [33]:
# Create the classifier
bayesClassifier = BinaryRelevance(
    MultinomialNB(), # Wrap MultinomialNB
    require_dense=[True, True] # Require dense to speed up our process (we have sparse matrices, especially for tf-idf)
)

# Fit the training data and predict on test set for tfidf
bayesClassifier.fit(X_train_tfidfVectorised, y_train)
y_predBayesTfidf = bayesClassifier.predict(X_test_tfidfVectorised)

# Fit the training data and predict on test set for GloVe
try:
    bayesClassifier.fit(X_train_GloVeVectorisedOutNA, y_trainGloVeVectorisedOutNA)
    y_predBayesGloVe = bayesClassifier.predict(X_test_GloVeVectorised)
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Negative value in the embedding, cannot proceed with Multinomial Bayes [{e}]")

Negative value in the embedding, cannot proceed with Multinomial Bayes [Negative values in data passed to MultinomialNB (input X)]

Here we can see that the bayes classifier worked on our tf-idf encoding (which can be interpreted in some way as a count). Unfortunately, this is not the case for GloVe, which posses negatives values in document embedding that can therefore not be interpreted as a count, making the Classifier fails for this representation. We will therefore use another baseline: the closeness to the average embedding (Nearest neighbour in a sense):

In [34]:
class ClosenessDocEmbeddingClassifier():
    def __init__(self):
        pass
    
    def fit(self, X_train:np.ndarray[float], Y_train:np.ndarray[int]) -> None:
        # Initialise the label embedding
        self.averageEmbedding = {}
        
        # For each label
        for label in range(Y_train.shape[1]):
            # Find which rows has this label
            inLabel = np.where(Y_train[:,label])[0]
            
            # Take the average of document possessing it
            self.averageEmbedding[label] = np.mean(X_train[inLabel,:], axis=0)
    
    def calibrateThreshold(self, X_dev:np.ndarray[float], Y_dev:np.ndarray[int], precision:int=10**4, verbose:bool = True) -> None:
        # Cut the space [0,1] to precision slice (to test all the thresholds)
        thresholds = np.linspace(0,1,precision)
        
        # Register the best Hamming similarity
        bestHamming = np.full(len(self.averageEmbedding.keys()), -1, dtype=float)
        self.thresholds = np.full(len(self.averageEmbedding.keys()), -1, dtype=float)
        begin = time.time()
        
        # For each threshold
        for i, threshold in enumerate(thresholds):
            # Warn the user if necessary
            if verbose and i%1000 == 0:
                print(f"[{time.time()-begin:.5f}s] threshold: {i}/{precision}")
            
            # Create the predicted matrix as 0
            Y_pred = np.zeros_like(Y_dev, dtype=int)
            
            # For each label
            for label, labelEmbedding in self.averageEmbedding.items():
                # Compute the cosine similarity
                labelCos = GloVe.getCosineSimilarity(X_dev,labelEmbedding)
                
                # Fill the prediction
                Y_pred[np.where(labelCos>=threshold)[0], label] = 1
                
                # Take Hamming similarity for each label and store it if it is the best
                if 1 - hamming_loss(Y_dev[:,label], Y_pred[:,label]) > bestHamming[label]:
                    self.thresholds[label] = threshold
    
    def predict(self, X_test:np.ndarray[float]) -> np.ndarray[int]:
        # Initialise the predicted matrix as zeros
        Y_pred = np.zeros((X_test.shape[0], len(self.averageEmbedding.keys())), dtype=int)
        
        # For each labels
        for label, labelEmbedding in self.averageEmbedding.items():
            
            # Compute cosine similarity
            labelCos = GloVe.getCosineSimilarity(X_test, labelEmbedding)
            
            # Make predictions 
            Y_pred[np.where(labelCos>=self.thresholds[label])[0], label] = 1
        
        # Return the prediction
        return Y_pred

Now, we can make our predictions for GloVe. Note that the hyperparameter tuning is done using weighted F1-Score because of the imbalance in each labels and the biggest importance granted to more frequent labels.

Warning: since this can be long and/or memory intensive, you can go to the next restoration point for the results.

In [ ]:

embeddingClassifier.calibrateThreshold(X_dev_GloVeVectorised, y_dev)

# Predict the results
y_predEmbeddingGloVe = embeddingClassifier.predict(X_test_GloVeVectorised)

Report¶

Now that we have computed all the baseline, we should evaluate them. Usually, we tend to show the confusion matrix, accuracies, precision, recall and F1-score. Unfortunately, this is not really doable in the context of multilabel classification. Indeed, a confusion matrix with all crossing would be too big (2**27 rows), one aggregated with the confusion matrix of all the label too misleading.

For accuracy, we can not really say that a combination of genres is false because one over seven is missing or that one is predicted despite not being present. Still, we can compare accuracy prediction for each labels. In the end, we will do this analysis:

  • Per label: Accuracy, F1-Score, Precision, Recall
  • Per rows: Jaccard similarity, Hamming Similarity, label accuracy product.

Here, we will not reexplain what accuracy, F1-Score, Precision and Recall are, but we will motivate the usages of the aggregation we will use.

First, the Jaccard similarity is computed as $J(Y,\hat{Y})=\frac{\#Y\cap \hat{Y}}{\#Y\cup\hat{Y}}$ where $\hat{Y}$ is the predicted genres and $Y$ the real genres. This metric is valued to 1 if the sets are identical, 0 if they are disjoint. It is convenient as it penalise both adding unnecessary genres, but also the absence of some. To get a value for the whole test set, we will average the rows Jaccard similarity.

Second, the Hamming "Similarity" that we will define as $\bar{H}(Y,\hat{Y}) = 1 - \frac{H(Y,\hat{Y})}{\#Y}$ where $H$ is the Hamming distance measuring the number of differences. This metric is values at 1 if there is no differences between the vector and at 0 if all is different. The difference with the Jaccard similarity is that it is sensitive to the number of 0, i.e. the sparser the vector, the more biaised the result. As for Jaccard, we will take the average.

Finally, we will proceed with the product of accuracies per label. In a sense, if I can predict with an accuracy of 0.9 the genre Action and 0.7 the genre Fantasy and ..., then by making the product, we would take into account all the error. Unfortunately, it could be less meaningful compared to the other metrics as it will quickly collapse to 0 considering the number of label to predict (example: 90% of accuracy over all label -> $0.9^{27}\approx0.0581$).

Let first proceed with the classic metric per labels.

In [37]:
# Function to compute the metrics
def computeLabelMetrics(y_true:np.ndarray[int], y_pred:np.ndarray[int], classes_:list[str]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # Initialise the dataframe
    genreMetrics = pd.DataFrame(columns=["Genre", "Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1-Score"])
    
    # If it is a sparse matrix, convert it back into array
    if not isinstance(y_pred, np.ndarray):
        y_pred = y_pred.toarray()
    
    # For each label
    for label in range(y_true.shape[1]):
        # Compute the metrics
        labelMetric = [
            classes_[label],
            accuracy_score(y_true[:,label], y_pred[:,label]),
            precision_score(y_true[:,label], y_pred[:,label], zero_division=np.nan),
            recall_score(y_true[:,label], y_pred[:,label]),
            f1_score(y_true[:,label], y_pred[:,label])
        ]
        # Register it
        genreMetrics.loc[label] = labelMetric
    
    # Return the dataframe
    return genreMetrics

# Compute the metrics for TFIDF over the 3 classifiers
labelMetricsBayesTfidf = computeLabelMetrics(y_test, y_predBayesTfidf, classes_)
labelMetricsLogisticTfidf = computeLabelMetrics(y_test, y_predLogisticTfidf, classes_)
labelMetricsEmbeddingTfidf = computeLabelMetrics(y_test, y_predEmbeddingTfidf, classes_)

# Compute the metrics for GloVe over the two classifiers
labelMetricsLogisticGloVe = computeLabelMetrics(y_test, y_predLogisticGloVe, classes_)
labelMetricsEmbeddingGloVe = computeLabelMetrics(y_test, y_predEmbeddingGloVe, classes_)

From the global results, we observe this in terms of accuracy:

  • GloVe Embedding and TFIDF under similarities classifier are not convincing. Indeed, even though accuracies are high, it is solely the fact that we correctly predict the true negative (which are majoritarian by the way). In the end, the classifier did only predict 0 for everyone, which is sufficient for high accuracies.
  • Bayes is already quite good at more than 70% of accuracy in general, Logistic being slightly better.

For F1-Score, we do not observe anything outstanding (apart from the embedding classifier which have a recall of 0, because of the already unveiled problem). Still, the F1-Score, in opposite to accuracy, is not particularly high. This could be explain by the imbalance in our label distribution we already had in the beginning. We also observe that GloVe is performing significantly worser than TFIDF, thus confirming again that our document embedding are not a good idea (averaging GloVe embedding for all token, made the semantics disappear).

Concerning the precision and recall, the precision is average, but the recall is bad; this indicates the difficulty in our model to correctly identify true positive.

For the further analysis, we will therefore drop the GloVe representation and stay with TFIDF. We will also drop th€Embedding model from our analysis as it does worse than a simple Bayes model...

Now let's compute our row metrics.

In [41]:
# Function to compute the metrics
def computeRowMetrics(X_unprocessed:np.ndarray[str], y_true:np.ndarray[int], y_pred:np.ndarray[int], classes_:list[str]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # Initialise the dataframe
    observationMetrics = pd.DataFrame(columns=["Description", "Genres", "Predicted Genres", "Jaccard", "Hamming"])
    classes_ = np.array(classes_)
    
    # If it is a sparse matrix, convert it back into array
    if not isinstance(y_pred, np.ndarray):
        y_pred = y_pred.toarray()
    
    # Compute the metric for each observations
    for i, description in enumerate(X_unprocessed):
        rowMetric = [
            description,
            list(classes_[np.where(y_true[i,:])[0]]),
            list(classes_[np.where(y_pred[i,:])[0]]),
            jaccard_score(y_true[i,:], y_pred[i,:]),
            1 - hamming_loss(y_true[i,:], y_pred[i,:])
        ]
    
        # Register it
        observationMetrics.loc[i] = rowMetric
    
    # Return the dataframe
    return observationMetrics.sort_values("Jaccard", ascending = False)
In [42]:
rowMetricsBayesTFIDF = computeRowMetrics(np.ravel(X_test[:,:,0]), y_test, y_predBayesTfidf, classes_)
rowMetricsLogisticTFIDF = computeRowMetrics(np.ravel(X_test[:,:,0]), y_test, y_predLogisticTfidf, classes_)

Observing these tables, we clearly see that Hamming is not a good metric (the quartile are too high and too close to be good with the remarks we had earlier on this metric). Concerning Jaccard, we do observe a significant difference in the median between Bayes and Logistic, Logistic having higher 2nd quartile and 3rd quartile. The mean for Logistic is also lower than the median, indicating that the distribution is skewed to the left. Still, the mean and standard deviation are very close, which is not a good sign of precision at all. Moreover, the Jaccard Index is only of 32.8% on average, which is still low; thus indicating over predication or misprediction. In our case, it is probably misprediction.

As we predicted, this measure is almost collapsed on 0%; so considering cumulative errors, the global accuracy of our system is 2% for Logistic and 1.79% for Bayes, thus representing an improvement of 12%.

Note that this result is what motivated the passage to non-perfect match metrics like Jaccard similarity. Indeed, lower values are not dramatic, as we do not expect perfect matches (otherwise, it would be near impossible for us, computationally speaking), in fact, depending on where you find you WN/LN description the displayed genres might very well change, so it is not a big problem (since no one is agreeing to genres in the first place).

Before improving our system, let us observe why did some description failed to be classified. We will analyse ten of them for Bayes and ten of them on Logistic. Let start with Bayes.

To begin with, each inferred genre, in the 10 worse classifications, were, either Fantasy, Romance or Action. Considering the massive input in Romance and Fantasy, it seems that the Bayes classifier did, in fact, put almost everyone in these categories.

When reading the descriptions, we have the following observation:

  • [799]: We observe the words transmigrated, wife, Male, hug and book, which are usually signals of a classic Romance/Isekai, which are traditionally in a Fantasy setting. Here the fantasy is replaced by the Historical and Supernatural.
  • [803]: The words transmigrated, novel, villain, plot and story, appearing in the description, are particularly important here. Indeed, they usually refers to the I was reincarnated as the villainess and must survive trope, which are usually tied to Romance and Fantasy. Here, there is the Yaoi tag which is related to the Romance tag in some way. For the others tags, none were actually inferable from the description itself.
  • [809]: (What a weird description) The key words here are: Beautiful, Love and Heart. Here the attributed genres are directly related, unfortunately, we observe a confusion between the tags Yaoi and romance. As for the fantasy tag, it does not really appears in some way (personally, I would have put Supernatural here, as it does more speaks of the peach boy legend in Japanese lore).
  • [821]: When reading the description, we have dialogues, expressions and clinical terms (which are filtered out), in the end, we have the words Female and Marry, which are clearly biased toward Romance even though the story is clearly not. (Sounds to be a good story to be honest).
  • [829]: Here, as the description says, this is a compilation of different stories, in consequence the Slice of Life label was just not inferred, because here, it is not really the story which is tell, but a description of the book, this make discrimination difficult. I suppose that, for safety, the classifier did classify to the most frequent classes.
  • [830]: Here, we do think the same happened, the classifier did make a default choice.
  • [832]: Here, the description does not provide any useful information related to our genres.
  • [839]: Again, we observe the confusion between Romance and Yaoi. We suppose that in description, Yaoi and Fantasy are not really different considering that most of the time Yaoi tends to be more "explicit", but they cannot put it in the eye of the large public.
  • [846]: (That's weird, help! I do not want to analyse these anymore) Same confusion, but failed to capture the Supernatural/Fantasy context, which could have been captured in the token party which is usually used for Guild/Adventure/Fantasy context.
  • [1209]: Here, we observe a completely different context, we have the words Zombie, Area, Virus, People and Fighting, which clearly reflect Action (properly inferred), despite the genre not being in the attributed list. Fantasy could also have been a good guess here (despite being a bit surprising), so in this situation, we think it is more related to bad genres attributions/bad description.

Here we observe a tendency among the errors, it is usually classic context and setup, but approached from an alternative point of view. This seems to have tendencies to destabilize our model. Additionally, some tags are very close, so it could be a good idea to adresses this issue with rule mining or fuzzy links in evaluation (For example, if I match Yaoi, then I automatically match Romance at 70% for example).

Here, we observe in general that Fantasy is less inferred than with Bayes (maybe because we broke the independence hypothesis with Bayes before...). For the errors, we have the following:

  • [1209]: Already analysed before, lost his Fantasy tag, which seems coherent.
  • [354]: Here, the description is too concise to infer anything.
  • [1023]: We find again the confusion between Mature/Yaoi and Romance. Still considering the rebirth token appearing multiple time, it is bizarre to not observe the Fantasy tag.
  • [344]: We suspect here that the combination of tag is quite rare here. There is again some token for Romance, but it is too light...
  • [340]: There is the words Marrying, Brother-in-law, bride-to-be and seduce, which usually convey the Romance tag. Death can also be tied to Isekai -> Fantasy, but here it is not figurative, but real, hence the tag Horror. In the end, we have the polysemic nature of words which entrave the real meaning.
  • [1029]: We find the words Adventurer and Class which are usually tied to the duo Fantasy/Action. Here, only the Fantasy was inferred; still, we do not have explanation (apart from the high number of Romance in the training data) to the presence of Romance tag here.
  • [1032]: Here the Logistic regression, did something bizarre by placing it into Comedy, while nothing explains it. For Romance it is maybe a bit more understandable with high-schooler which is tied to the duo School-Life/Romance, but it is not a strong explanation.
  • [1033]: Here, we have no way to predict correctly the tag Yaoi (there is no sign in the description). Moreover, the story in itself is quite original (the context of airplane crash investigation is rare); this could explain why we could not predict tags at all.
  • [325]: Here, we have the tokens Bully, Hate, Dead, which are clearly related to Action and Vengeance, so not a bad guess here. Nonetheless, it could not have guesses the Yaoi or Romance tag here, but there was clear sign of Supernatural.
  • [324]: Here, we are faced with the classic trope: "I was saved by someone and fall in love with him". This is classic in description, still they base themself into hidden "Implied Knowledge" (like 2nd degré in French or knowledge which is not explicite, because assumed known by everyone).

Here we have clearly seen that the model is much less lost between classic confusions, but have problems for rare combination of genres or unexpected ones. It also have problems on implied and underlying knowledge.

4.2 - Neural Model¶

In our case, we already seen that using pre-trained GloVe embedding was not a proper approach. Additionally, TF-IDF does not capture the context behind the tokens. Considering the results of the logistic regression, we do not expect higher results which classical Neural Network approach on TF-IDF. For this reason, we will start over from scratch to use BERT Embedding along with Neural Networks.

Let us start with loading the models:

In [50]:

inputs = tokenizerBert(
    ["This is a test. And this is testing other things.", "Clearly peculiar, isn'it?"],
    return_tensors="pt",   # PyTorch

# Get the output

In [52]:
def getBertEmbedding(Xset:np.ndarray[str], batchSize:int = 25) -> list[list[float]]:

    # Initialise the list that will contains the embeddings
    Xset_embedded = []
    begin = time.time()

    # Put the Bert Model in evaluation mode
    modelBert.eval()
    # For each batch
    for i in range(0, (Xset.shape[0]/batchSize).__ceil__()):
        # Tokenize the batch
        XsetBertTokenized = tokenizerBert(
            # Get str to always have a valid sequence
            list(map(str, Xset[i*batchSize:(i+1)*batchSize,0])),
            return_tensors="pt",
            padding=True, 
            truncation=True
        )
        # Print the advancement
        if i%10 == 0:
            print(f"Batch no. {i}/{(Xset.shape[0]/batchSize).__ceil__()} [{time.time()-begin:.4f}s]")
        
        # Get the embedding
        with torch.no_grad():
            Xset_embedded.extend(modelBert(**{k:v.to("cuda") for k,v in XsetBertTokenized.items()}).last_hidden_state[:,0,:].tolist())
        
    return Xset_embedded

Now that everything seems to work, we will proceed with Neural Networks. Note that before achieving the following network, multiple undisplayed iterations were made. Here is the Neural Network we will use:

In [55]:
class NeuralMultiLabelClassifier(nn.Module):
    # 768: dimension of the BERT embedding, 27: dimension of the label space
    def __init__(self, input_dim:int=768, num_labels:int=27, refine:bool = False):
        super().__init__()
        
        # Main component to identify the features (input)
        self.feature = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, 512),
            nn.LayerNorm(512),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Dropout(0.3)
        )
        
        # Output layer
        self.classifier = nn.Linear(512, num_labels)
        
        # Linear Correlation learning module + the weight we will derive in the logits
        self.label_correlation = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(num_labels, num_labels, bias=False),
            nn.Tanh()
        )
        self.corr_gate = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(0.5))
        
        # Refining layer (is active only if correlation is not). Used to capture higher correlation relationships between labels 
        self.addRefine = refine
        self.refine = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(512 + num_labels, 256),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(256, num_labels)
        )

    # Feed forward function
    def forward(self, x):
        # Get the feetures
        h = self.feature(x)
        # Classify
        logits = self.classifier(h)
        
        # Add the correlation between the labels
        if not self.addRefine:
            logits = logits + self.corr_gate*self.label_correlation(logits)
        else:
            logits = logits + self.refine(torch.cat([h, logits], dim=1))
        return logits

Now, we have to explain and justify our architecture. The architecture itself is divided into 3 consecutive parts:

  • The Feature layer: constitute the hidden layer to learn the features associated to each token. It make use of three main part: a dense layer (to learn the components), a normalisation layer (to stabilise the model and make sure to reach convergence), a GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit) activation function, which apparently boost the performances in transformer contextes, as suggested here (BERT use a transformer, so it seems coherent to use this activation function here), as well as a dropout layer of 30% to avoid overfitting (this dropout is used because we have a rather simple model and that standard values range between 20% and 50% as seen here; In a way, it could be a tunable parameter, but we will not exploit this here).
  • The Classifier layer: It is the layer in charge of connecting the networks to the 27 output labels. We do not perform softmax here as it would vanish the possibility to predict multiple labels at once. To interpret the results, we will have to find the best threshold for which we consider a genre to be acquired or not.
  • (Choice 1) The Correlation Layer: By passing through the two first layers, we ensured that we could use correlation between tokens, but this does not take into account the correlation between labels. This is why we apply this layer, to learn the correlation between the label and apply the corrections to the results. Note that we use Tanh afterward for the same reason of normalisation (between -1 and 1 here to respect the correlation meaning); also, the potential noise created by this layer is mitigated using a parameter that can be learned. Basically, this layer say: "If I increase A, then I should increase/decrease B".
  • (Choice 2) The Refinement Layer: By doing the refinement layer instead of the correlation layer, we do not limit ourself to direct correlation, but we also investigate non-linear deeper pattern (like conditional patterns or multi-correlated patterns). Hence, the dense layer with the dimension 512+27 to take the features and labels into account.

In the end, we have an architecture like this:

  1. Raw documents
  2. Bert Embeddings
  3. Feature Layer
  4. Classifier Layer
  5. Correlation | Refinement Layer
  6. Sigmoid (prediction)
  7. Thresholds (to go back to binary)

For the tunable parameters, we have the dropout rate (we will not touch it), but more importantly the thresholds. Each output may have a different distribution per se. As a consequence, we cannot set a global threshold like IF pred>0.5 THEN PREDICT 1; it does not make sense, additionally, this would not take into account the label imbalance which is probably the biggest challenge here as we will explain.

Now that we explained the architecture, let us normalise our embeddings:

Now, we proceed with the training loop. Here, we will do the training for both model with correlation layer and refinement layer.

In [57]:
def trainNN(X_train:torch.tensor, Y_train:torch.tensor, batchSize:int = 100, epochs:int=50, refine:bool=True, seed:int=0) -> NeuralMultiLabelClassifier:
    # Setup the seed of torch for reproducibility
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    
    # Because the labels are unbalanced, use the Weighted BCEWithLogitLoss so that we can add a higher weight to rare labels
    positiveCount = Y_train.sum(axis=0)
    negativeCount = Y_train.shape[0] - positiveCount
    positiveWeight = negativeCount / positiveCount
    criterion = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=torch.tensor(positiveWeight))
    
    # Initialise the Neural Model
    neuralModel = NeuralMultiLabelClassifier(refine=refine)
    
    # Use classic Adam with classic learning rate
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(neuralModel.parameters(), lr=1e-4)

    # Start the training loop
    begin = time.time()
    neuralModel.train()
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        # Inform of the advancement
        if epoch%10 == 0:
            print(f"[{time.time()-begin:.3f}s] {epoch=}")
        
        # Permute the batches at each epoch to avoid Overfitting. The random seed is set to epoch to keep determinism
        rng = np.random.RandomState(epoch)
        permutation = rng.permutation(np.arange(X_train.shape[0]))
        X_epoch = X_train[permutation]
        Y_epoch = Y_train[permutation]
        
        # For each batch
        for batch in range(0, (X_train.shape[0]/batchSize).__ceil__()):
            # Reinitialise gradient
            optimizer.zero_grad()

            # Compute logits and loss for the current batch
            logits = neuralModel(torch.tensor(X_epoch[batch*batchSize:(batch+1)*batchSize,:]))
            loss = criterion(logits, torch.tensor(Y_epoch[batch*batchSize:(batch+1)*batchSize]).float())

            # Back propagation
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
    
    # Return the model
    return neuralModel

Like we said earlier, we have two main challenges for this classification task: the high correlation between the labels (already address with the architecture) and the label imbalance observed at the very beginning of this project.

For this balance problem, we use a particular Loss function: Weighted Binary Cross Entropy with Logits, as suggested here. For the weight, we use an inverse weight on positive labels to prioritize rare labels over frequent one (to not fall on the same error we had with GloVe embedding earlier where rare labels were never predicted).

For the optimizer, we stayed with the classic Adam and a standard learning rate.

To avoid overfitting, we only train for 50 epochs (which seems correct for a simple model like this one) and permute the order of the batches at every new epochs to avoid learning an order/pattern within the batches. The seed of the permutation is set to the epoch value to keep the reproducibility.

Now that it is done, we can talk about one of the most important part: the threshold tuning.

In [59]:
def tuneOutputThresholds(y_true:np.ndarray[int], y_pred:np.ndarray[int], classes_:list[str], precision:float=10**4) -> np.ndarray[float]:
    thresholds = []
    begin = time.time()

    # For each label
    for label in range(y_true.shape[1]):
        # Initialise the threshold and MacroF1 (we use macroF1 because of class imbalances)
        bestThreshold, bestF1 = 0.5, 0

        # For each threshold
        for threshold in np.linspace(0, 1, precision):
            # Make the prediction based on the threshold
            preds = (y_pred[:, label] > threshold).astype(int)

            # Compute the MacroF1 for the given label
            f1 = f1_score(y_true[:,label], preds, average="macro")

            # If it is the best F1-Score, update the threshold
            if f1 > bestF1:
                bestF1 = f1
                bestThreshold = threshold

        # Register the final threshold
        thresholds.append(bestThreshold)
        
        # Inform the user
        print(f"[{time.time()-begin:.4f}s] Label {label+1}/{y_true.shape[1]} ({classes_[label]}) done. Best threshold: {bestThreshold:.6f}")

    # Return the thresholds as numpy arrays
    return np.array(thresholds)

For the threshold tuning, we simply find the thresholds (with 0.0001 precision), such that the F1-Score for particular labels are maximised. Each labels having its own threshold to match their own distribution.

Note that we do not use Accuracy for the tuning. Indeed, we already saw that accuracy was not a good metric when examining GloVe, from this constat, we use F1-Score which is more resistant to class imbalance. Initially, we used to maximize the Jaccard Index, but it revealed to be counterproductive by penalising too much False Positive on rare label, thus leading to no prediction on rare labels.

Figure

From the cumulative distribution function of the different models created so far, we observe that Bayes and Logistic over TFIDF perform the worst overall. For both BERT methods, we do not observer significant difference between those; still, their performance are better than the baseline. If we observe the median of the Jaccard similarity, we observe an improvement of 20.84% for BERT Corr compared to Logistic TFIDF. This difference is even more impressive on the 1st quartile with an improvement of 44.1% from both compared to Logistic.

Note: By changing the seed, we did observe that BERT Refined was better sometimes, so we would say there is not much difference between the two models.

We can also try to visualise our embedding to see if the environment was easily separable or not depending on the labels. For that, we will use TSNE, a technique for dimensionality reduction that conserve distances between points, in order to observe a 768-dimension vector into a 2-dimensional plain.

    'Seinen':        (255, 215, 0),     
    'Josei':         (255, 215, 0),    
    'Slice of life': (255, 215, 0),    
}

def colourY(y_train:np.ndarray[int], classes_:np.ndarray[str], genre_colours:dict[str,tuple[int]]) -> list[tuple[int,int,int]]:
    # Just asked chat gpt to define "coherent" colour for each genres
    # https://stackoverflow.com/questions/649454/what-is-the-best-way-to-average-two-colors-that-define-a-linear-gradient

    colourValue = []
    for i in range(y_train.shape[0]):
        # Get the colours to the corresponding genres
        values = [genre_colours[genre] for genre in classes_[np.where(y_train[i,:])[0]]]
        r, g, b = 0, 0, 0
        
        if len(values) == 0:
            colourValue.append((1,1,1,0))
            continue        
        
        # Comput the Root Mean Squared colour (simple average would be to fade)
        for ri, gi, bi in values:
            r+=ri**2
            g+= gi**2
            b+=bi**2
        
        # Append a normalised value between 0 and 1
        colourValue.append([
            min(max(((r/len(values))**0.5)/255,0),1), 
            min(max(((g/len(values))**0.5)/255,0),1),
            min(max(((b/len(values))**0.5)/255,0),1),
            1/len(values)
        ])
    return colourValue

# Plot the results
    
plt.close("all")
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))

# The legend logic was produced by ChatGPT (we had no clues on how to do this with matplotlib).
def normalize(rgb):
    return tuple(v / 255 for v in rgb)

legend_elements = []
labels = []

# Create the legend
for genre, color in genre_colours.items():
    legend_elements.append(
        Line2D(
            [0], [0],
            marker='o',
            linestyle='',
            markerfacecolor=normalize(color),
            markeredgecolor='black',
            markersize=8
        )
    )
    labels.append(genre)

# Plot the points with the defined colour
plt.scatter(embeddingTrainVisualisation[:,0], embeddingTrainVisualisation[:,1], c=np.array(colourY(y_train, classes_, genre_colours)))
plt.title("The more a point is transparent, the more genres are associated with it.")
plt.suptitle("Average genre for each BERT embedding of the training set")

# Show the built legend
plt.legend(
    handles=legend_elements,
    labels=labels,
    title="Genres",
    loc='best',
    ncol=2,
    fontsize=8
)
# Plot the diagrams
plt.show()
Figure

From this plot, we clearly see that this task was not trivial. Some genres are heavily convoluted with others, some entries possess way more labels than other, and so on. Still, by choosing the colour wisely and putting a malus on the number of genres, which is basically the same as rewarding "pure" genres (only Fantasy, or only Adventure and so on); we can capture some informations:

  1. The Romance & co family is universal and do not tends towards a particular place.
  2. The Slice of Life & co family is also distributed evenly except a blob higher in the sphere where it can be seen as "purer". In the other side, it is also frequently associated to Romance as seen in the very middle of the sphere.
  3. The Fantasy family is fitted at the center; this make sense because Fantasy and co are frequently an environment associated to other genres. Such a frequent co-occurrences of genres are Fantasy and Romance.
  4. Finally, Martial Arts and Shounen do emerges, but in a very small part.

6. Error Analysis & Interpretation¶

In this part, we will compare all the models, in terms of performances and committed errors.

First, let's regroup all the results we had earlier:

Figure

Now, what can be said about those ?

First, the median of the Hamming Similarity is almost always the same and does not seems significative. Indeed as we told earlier, the Hamming similarity is very sensitive to the size of the label space and since on average, we do not have much labels, this metric favours the huge amount of zero in our vector, which is not good if we want to predict rare labels.

Second, the accuracy product is always low, it is normal, because it actually correspond to the probability of having a perfect match, and with 27 labels, it is not probable. Still, we observe that our Neural models, for which we focused to have better rare label prediction, have a lower chance of perfect matches. Again, this is logical, as we encourage the inference of rare labels, which cut the perfect match in case of mistake.

Third, the median Jaccard similarity remains decent overall, with embedding similarity as a caveat where the median Jaccard similarity is 0 (we have seen earlier that the results with this predictor were basically highest frequencies). The best results are still achieved with our Neural models, even though Bayes and Logistics return decent results as well.

In the end, we would like to see if there is a significant difference in label inferences (is there different strategies) or if our Neural model are just bumped Bayes/Logistic classifiers.

For that, we can take a looks at the other metrics per label.

Concerning the accuracy per labels, we first see that document embeddings similarity approaches (GloVe and co) generally leads to the best accuracy, because its classification really approaches the "most frequent label" classifier. This also mean something important: since accuracy is high considering this fact, then the matter is no longer the accuracy, but the right classification of label combination and rare labels (we are most interested in Precision, Recall and F1-Score in our case, which are more resistant to label imbalance). On whether the Neural approaches is better with respect to accuracy disregarding embedding similarities, we do not observe significant differences to other methods.

From the F1-Score perspective, the scores are generally mediocre (below 50% most of the time), but we do observe significant differences between our baselines and the neural models. While the results are comparable for most frequent labels like Fantasy and Romance, the neural models clearly outperform baselines on genres likes Shoujo (approximately +0.3 points), Supernatural (approximately +0.3), Sci-Fi (approximately +0.3), Yaoi (approximately +0.25), Historical (approximately +0.25), which are representatives of rarer genres or more convoluted ones (eg. confusion between Romance/Yaoi or Supernatural/Fantasy); this is good news because it means, at first glance, that we were able to more easily discriminate the genres and break the ambiguity between some related ones. As for if there is a difference between the two Neural models, we do not strictly observe an ascendant from one to another on the basis of F1-Score alone. But is the reason why F1-Score are similar between those two model the same? Let us see through Precision and Recall.

For Precision, the results are quite varying depending on the labels. First of all, the best precision is often achieve by the baselines. This is interesting, because it means that our baselines tends to correctly classify positives among, while our neural models are quite struggling with. Still, as said earlier, some genres have very poor precision: Yaoi, Supernatural, Shoujo, Josei, while others have strong ones: Romance, Fantasy, Action. In the end, we could probably attribute these results to the semantic correlation that is unveiled by those genres. For the differences between the two neural models, the BERT Corr model obtains globally better precision, even though it is slight and does not display particular advantages regarding the type of genres.

Regarding the Recall, the story is widely different. Indeed, traditional approaches tends to have recalls closer to zero (Adult, Ecchi, Harem, Historical, Horror, ...), while being completely dominated by neural approaches in all categories, except Fantasy and Romance, with a minimal gap of approximately 0.08 points of recall for Action and the biggest over 0.5 points of recall. This is interesting, because this truly show that our neural models better capture the positives than our baseline; in other words, it shows that imbalance and correlation between labels should be took into account when doing inferences. Concerning whether a particular neural method is better for recall, we observe that none is truly better than the other; nonetheless, the results are somehow widely different, thus indicating that higher order correlation (refined) or simple correlation efficiencies deeply depend on the embedding tested. It would be interesting to identify those cases, where one is better than the others.

Now we will take a look at the worse classification error we made with our baselines and determine whether going to neural models helps.

(The id were: 324, 325, 340, 344, 354, 799, 803, 809, 821, 829, 830, 832, 839, 846, 1029, 1032, 1033, 1202, 1209)

Now that we have these results, what can we observe with these results?

First of all, except for the entry 803, all the classification made by both models were strictly at least as better as the one made by our baseline. Secondly, BERTCorr was in general better than BERTRefined. Thirdly, the neural models tends to infer more labels than our baselines (probably because we took the correlations of labels into consideration).

Now, what about the Romance/Yaoi (803, 839, 846) and the Supernatural/Fantasy (799) confusions we made with our baselines?

  • [803]: For this one, the confusion between Yaoi and Romance is still clear, but contrary to Bayes, which put only one of those, the neural models took into account the correlation and put both. This warranty at least something to be true and therefore have a Jaccard Index over 0. Still Logistic is better here as it has the tendency to put less labels.
  • [839]: Here, we observe something interesting, despite BERTCorr predicting only half of the real answer, BERTRefined did produce a superset of the real answer. When we check the additional labels, we also observe that they make sense; indeed, the words devil, underground, memory and secret can clearly be associated to Tragedy, Mature or Mystery. In the end, the neural models would have inferred something closer to what, we, humans, could have inferred by reading the description.
  • [799]: As observed in the newly inferred labels, the confusion for Supernatural/Fantasy was not solved. Still, the results are interesting because the inferred labels are straight to what a human would have done. The Josei tag was correctly inferred, as well as the Romance tag, which could have been correct by reading the description.
  • [846]: Here, the same remarks as what as been told for (803) can be done.

And what about particular descriptions, using implicit knowledge (324), having short descriptions (354), or having a description of the staff/material instead of story itself (829)?

  • [324]: Now, the results are very interesting. In this example, the baselines were not able to correctly infer the "I got rescued by a saviour, I fell in love directly after"; but the neural models did. In addition to just infer Romance as Bayes did, they also correctly inferred Josei and Mature (but not Adult). Reading the description, Historical, Drama and Martial Art were also plausible, so it is not really a problem to predict them. This example show that neural models can capture some implicit knowledge through common tropes (probably thanks to the contextual embedding of BERT).
  • [354]: With this example, even though we correctly predicted part of the answer; we do not see any improvement versus Bayes. In the end, we cannot infer the genres properly with such shorts descriptions.
  • [829]: Here, nothing really new. We managed to infer Slice Of Life with BERTCorr, but this is probably more a lucky guess than a real one. If the description does not talk about the story, we cannot infer the tags of it.

So, in the end, we showed that both neural models help mitigate the Romance/Yaoi confusion, without eliminating it completely, can capture implicit knowledge, but is still limited to the description type (length and if it talk about the story or not).

The only question remaining is: where does the neural models fails? Let's first begin with BERTCorr.

This result is reasonable and should not destroy our results and observation. Now back to the other description:

  • [96]: In this description, the format is quite special and more shaping a poem than a description, making it very original. From it, BayseCorr made good guesses (I would probably have inferred something similar), but we can see a confusion appearing between Historical and Martial Arts/Xuanhuan, which are frequently inferred together.
  • [1061]: Even though I tend to be formal in reports, excuse me for this, but WTF is this: the Joker (DC Comics) and Sherlock Holmes being in a mental Hospital managed by the SCP foundation (weird meme of the internet). Obviously, it has to be Comedy right? Unfortunately for the models, the real labels are Mystery and Supernatural (which seems right for the SCP foundation). To infer these labels, we have to know about the SCP foundation, which is itself hidden as an inside joke (meme) of the internet. It is not surprising that our models cannot infer these without this information.
  • [870]: The description is very short, but does contain somewhat useful information like Tombstone or Wolf that remind us of Supernatural. The length of the description probably amplified the Supernatural/Fantasy confusion.

Here, BERTRefined provide examples of failures on short description (823), confusion between Drama and Tragedy (1159), descriptions that are very long, but does not truly fit their attributed genres (66), confusion between Yaoi/Adult/Romance as well as Martial arts/Xuanhuan (1089) and another confusion between Adult/Mature/Romance and Josei (1073, do not read the description, it is awful).

In the end, we cannot neither really tell which neural model is better nor the particularities separating them. The only thing we can tell, is that, despite their visible differences on inferences, their failure points are the same: empty/short description, awkward labelling, particular format, production description instead of story description and descriptions that are very convoluted or needing particular knowledge/references to understand the mapping to there genres.

For potential biases, apart from those mentioned in the very beginning and the different confusions observed throughout the report, we did not detect particularly strong biases for theses classifiers. Still, Bayes had one by putting Romance or Fantasy everywhere.

Conclusion, Area for improvement and Academic Integrity Declaration¶

In this work, we navigated within the Web/Light Novel Dataset and applied different tools to predict the genres of a Web Novel/Light Novel from their description, including Bayes, Logistic, GloVe and BERT based methods. To achieve this, we extensively studied the links between the labels and how can this be leveraged in a context of highly imbalanced multilabelling task. In addition, we also reflects on the evaluation metrics in the case of multilabel classification, from the classic accuracy to the Jaccard index to move from perfect matches to more appropriate evaluation.

Along the way, we observed two main way to perform multilabel classification: Binary Relevance (one classifier per label), which is the simplest way, but cannot handle label correlations; as well as Neural Networks to leverage this correlation for better classification.

In the end, we were not able to produce a perfect-match model with high accuracy, but we did developed somewhat usable and satisfiable models without particularly visible biases: BERT Refined and BERT Correlation. Far from perfect, they nonetheless displayed convincing results, similar to what a human could have done in limiting context like wrong labelling, short description, inside jokes, production description and so on.

Concerning area of improvements, we clearly see four possible ways:

  1. Binary Relevance over Bayes or Logistic regression does not take into account correlation. It could be interesting to see whether inferring fuzzy association rules between labels could solve this issue. This would imply that labels are no longer fully True or False, but could take values from the range of 0 (fully false) and 1 (fully true). This hypothesis is interesting because it is closer to reality, but we would also have to find a fuzzification technique to do that (probably rule based too), which can be quite challenging.

  2. In this report, we only focused on genres; but actually, the dataset also contains tags (kind of subgenres). In this regard, it could be interesting to see if leveraging these tags could help us inferring the labels in one way or another. Nonetheless, this could be quite challenging with 891 additional subgenres with their own imbalance and correlations.

  3. In a similar wat, we could observe if including the title of the novel to the classification problem would change something; especially in the WN/LN industry, where titles like "I Was Reincarnated as the 7th Prince so I Can Take My Time Perfecting My Magical Ability" or "Is It Wrong to Try to Pick Up Girls in a Dungeon?" describing the plot are very common.

  4. We observed a lot of confusion between the tags. With this respect, we could try to merge more thoroughly genres into higher families; or take this confusion into account in the evaluation, saying for example: "If I infer Fantasy instead of Supernatural, it is as if I had inferred Supernatural at 70%." (Fuzzy evaluation). This could be interesting to try and would probably be one of the best way to represent overlapping non-semantically-mergeable genres (Adult!=Romance).
